title: Guest Experience & Review Strategy in the AI Ranking Era

slides.title: Run your rental on what Airbnb actually publishes about search, not on rumors
slides.subtitle: Lesson OP.9. Guest Experience & Review Strategy in the AI Ranking Era
meta: Education only. Platform policies change; check Airbnb's current pages.
slides.notes:
After this lesson you can tell what Airbnb actually says affects search apart from claims about "the algorithm." You'll map each factor to something you control, set up guest checkpoints, write a compliant review request, and start a monthly tracker.

So what's the "AI ranking era"? Airbnb doesn't publish whether or how AI changes its ranking. So I stick to what Airbnb does publish, and to the guest experience that shows up in reviews. I'm not promising a rank boost from any AI trick that Airbnb doesn't document.

Quick cast list. Cedar Ridge is a hypothetical lake house owned by Maya and Chris. Maya answers guest messages, so she's the message owner. Chris is her backup and gets the repair quotes. When I say "the owners," I mean the two of them.

Sam is the other instructor in this course. He teaches the live demos, including listing setup in OP.1 and OP.2, and pricing in OP.5. This lesson covers the operating side: the parts guests experience and then write about.

slides.title: Airbnb's search page names four main factors, plus variety and availability
items: Quality: photos and videos, ratings and reviews, host-guest communication, listing details
Popularity: how often guests save the listing to a wishlist, book it, and message the host
Price: total price vs. nearby listings; lower than similar listings tends to rank higher
Location: listings in places guests like to stay tend to rank higher
Plus variety: the system shows guests different hosts, characteristics, and prices
Plus availability: more open dates and flexible stay lengths help a listing fit more trips
slides.notes:
This is what Airbnb's search page says. I checked it in September 2026, and the details are in the sources.

Airbnb names four main factors. Quality, popularity, price, and location heavily influence how a listing appears. Quality looks at listing content like photos and videos, guest ratings and reviews, communication between hosts and guests, and listing characteristics.

Popularity looks at how guests engage: how often they save a listing to a wishlist, book it, and message the host.

Price looks at the total price and how it compares with other listings in the area. Listings priced below comparable listings with similar characteristics tend to rank higher.

Location matters a lot. Listings in places guests like to stay tend to rank higher.

Then the page adds two more points. The system encourages variety, so guests see different hosts and prices. And availability matters. The more dates a listing is open, the more likely it shows up. More flexibility on length of stay helps a listing fit more trips.

That's the published list. When someone tells you about a factor that isn't on it, ask them for the Airbnb page.

slides.title: The page gives no weights, so work on the factors you control day to day

left.head: What the page doesn't say
items: No weights for any factor
Nothing on which features count more this year than last
No mention of any special field for AI
If someone sells a trick, ask for the Airbnb page that supports it

right.head: Who controls what at Cedar Ridge
items: Location: fixed when Maya and Chris bought the house
Price: Sam's OP.5; don't cut price just for search
Popularity: grows from the others (first photo, title, total price, fast replies)
Quality: accurate content, clean stays, clear and fast communication, good reviews
Availability: open dates and stay lengths that fit your short-term rental permit

slides.notes:
Notice what's missing from Airbnb's page. It doesn't give weights. It doesn't say which features count more this year than last year. It doesn't mention any special field that AI reads.

So when a course or a consultant tells you the algorithm now rewards some specific trick, check it against the page. If they can't point you to the Airbnb page that says so, treat it as a guess.

Then sort the factors by who controls them. Location was fixed when Maya and Chris bought the house. Price belongs to Sam's OP.5 lesson on dynamic pricing. Ranking isn't the only goal of price, and OP.5 covers that trade-off. So don't cut your price just for search.

Popularity grows from the others: a clear first photo and title, an accurate total price, and fast replies.

Day to day, you control two things. You control quality: accurate content, clean stays, clear and fast communication, and the reviews that come from all that. And you control availability: open dates, and stay lengths that fit your short-term rental permit.

slides.title: Airbnb's four ground rules cover what guests tend to write about in reviews
items: Accuracy: describe the home truly; change a booking only with the guest's consent
Commitment: honor bookings, give a reliable check-in, cancel only for valid reasons
Communication: the host or co-host (a helper on the listing) is available before and during stays
Cleanliness: clean between every stay to a high standard

box.label: Airbnb enforces these
box.text: Airbnb enforces these. Actions can include education, warnings, and removing content that misrepresents the listing.

slides.notes:
Airbnb's ground rules for home hosts focus on four things.

Accuracy means the listing describes the home and the amenities available from check-in to checkout. You change an accepted booking's details only with the guest's consent.

Reservation commitment means you honor accepted reservations and provide a reliable check-in. You don't cancel confirmed reservations except for valid reasons outside your control.

Communication means the host or co-host, someone who helps run the listing, is available to respond to inquiries and unexpected issues, before and during stays.

Cleanliness means you clean between every stay to a high standard.

The same page says Airbnb enforces these rules. That can mean education, warnings, and requiring hosts to remove content that misrepresents the listing.

Now look at the list again. Accuracy, check-in, communication, cleanliness. Those are the same things guests tend to write about in reviews. So the ground rules are the minimum, and reviews measure how far above it you land. OP.6 and OP.8 were built to clear this floor.

slides.title: Each published factor maps to a job someone on the team already owns
rows: Photos match the house today; every listed amenity works; exact sleeping arrangement
Clean, accurate, well-communicated stays; neutral requests; fixes for repeats
Named message owner; response target; a person checks automated messages
Clear first photo and title, accurate total price, fast answers
Nightly rate, cleaning fee, and minimum stay together
Calendar open far enough ahead; minimum stays that fit demand and permit
Update the listing the day something changes
No host cancellations except safety or outside causes
Cleaner photographs every room; a missed clean gets escalated
slides.notes:
This is the map from what Airbnb publishes to what the Cedar Ridge team actually does. The last column says where each job is covered, or who does it.

Most rows point back to work you've already done. The room inventory from OP.6 is what makes the photos and amenities accurate. The role map from OP.7 names the message owner, which is Maya. The SOPs from OP.8 produce clean, well-communicated stays. That's where reviews come from.

A few rows point to Sam. Popularity depends heavily on the first photo, the title, and the total price, which he covers in OP.1 and OP.2. Price and availability are his OP.5 lesson. Bring back from OP.5 how your minimum stays are set, because that's where availability and your permit meet.

Accuracy runs both ways. Guests can filter by amenities. List what you have, so a filtered search can find you. Remove what you don't have, the same day it breaks. If the grill breaks on Tuesday, it comes off the listing on Tuesday.

slides.title: Plan a checkpoint at each moment a guest decides whether the stay is going well
rows: Party size matches; no sign of an event
Correct code; house ready per photo review
Guest got in; first impression; quick fixes
Damage, left items, anything guests struggled with
slides.notes:
A guest journey is the sequence of moments where a guest decides whether this stay is going well. I plan a checkpoint at each one. A checkpoint is a moment where the team checks something, instead of waiting for a complaint.

The message owner, Maya at Cedar Ridge, runs most of these. "Owners" means Maya and Chris together.

The arrival-evening message matters most. Problems caught that night get fixed during the stay. Problems found after checkout go straight into a review.

Two gaps to plan for. If a booking comes in less than 7 days out, send the trip-prep message at booking. If you see signs of an event at booking, follow the retained lesson 9.4 on avoiding parties.

Two checkpoints happen after the guest leaves. Within 24 hours, the owners read the cleaner's walk-through notes. Two or three days later, the thank-you and review request goes out.

And once a week, the owners review the friction log. That's the next slide.

slides.text: A question guests ask twice means the house needs a fix, and many bad reviews start as a repeat nobody fixed.
slides.support: Mark every guest question. "Where's the water shutoff?" twice: the house manual needs a line. "How do the bunk lights work?" twice: the lights need a label.
slides.notes:
The friction log is the simplest tool in this lesson.

Every time a guest asks a question, mark it. One question is harmless. "Where's the water shutoff?" asked once is fine. By the second time, it goes on the fix list, and the house manual needs a line.

"How do the bunk lights work?" asked twice means the lights need a label. That's the house being unclear.

Many negative reviews start as a repeated question nobody fixed. Something confused the first guest, and they asked. The second guest asked too. That's your moment to fix it. The third guest didn't ask. They wrote it in the review.

So the log is a weekly habit. The owners read it every week and look for repeats. A repeat gets a fix, with a name and a date. That same twice-in-a-quarter rule shows up in the tracker and the exercise. It's also what drives the Cedar Ridge bunk room decision in the worked example.

slides.title: Airbnb's review policy bans any trade, incentive, or pressure around a review
slides.keyline: Guest and host each have 14 days after checkout to submit a review.

left.head: What the policy forbids
items: Coordinating with, manipulating, extorting, rewarding (incentivizing), or pressuring anyone to shape a review
Giving or withholding a review for something of value: a discount, refund, reciprocal review, or a promise not to take negative action
Threatening a negative review to get compensation, a refund, or another incentive

right.head: What that means for your request
items: It's neutral: it invites a review and asks for honest feedback
It offers nothing and hints at no trade
It doesn't tell the guest what rating to give
My rule, beyond the policy text: don't ask for "five stars" at all

slides.notes:
After checkout, Airbnb prompts both guest and host to leave a review. According to Airbnb's review pages, each side has 14 days after checkout to submit one.

Airbnb's policy on authentic and trustworthy reviews sets the limits on how you ask. Hosts and guests may not coordinate with, manipulate, extort, incentivize, or pressure another person to influence a review. Reviews may not be given or withheld in exchange for something of value. That includes a discount, a refund, a reciprocal positive review, or a promise not to take negative action. And neither side may threaten a negative review to get compensation or a refund.

So the review request has to be neutral. It invites a review. It asks for honest feedback. It doesn't offer anything, hint at a trade, or tell the guest what rating to give.

I'd go a step further than the policy text. Don't ask for five stars at all. Naming the rating reads as pressure, and the policy prohibits pressure.

slides.title: A compliant request invites an honest review and asks to hear about problems directly

left.head: Send this, 2 or 3 days after checkout
items: "Hi [first name], thanks for staying at Cedar Ridge. If you have a few minutes, we'd appreciate an honest review on Airbnb. If anything wasn't right, please tell us directly too, so we can fix it for the next guests."
Private feedback is in addition to the review, never instead of it

right.head: Never write this
items: "Leave us 5 stars and we'll give you a discount next time." (Incentive)
"We'll return your deposit once you've left a review." (Trade)
"We gave you a great review; we hope you'll do the same." (Reciprocal pressure)
Any goodwill gesture tied to review timing, such as a credit in the same message as the request

slides.notes:
Here's a request that works within the rules. It goes out two or three days after checkout. That gap gives the cleaner's notes time to come in, so you know about any problem before you ask.

It thanks them, invites an honest review, and asks them to tell you directly if anything wasn't right. That last line gives an unhappy guest a place to say it, and it gives you something to fix. Private feedback is in addition to the review, never instead of it.

The right column shows what never to write. The discount for five stars is an incentive. The deposit returned after a review is a trade. "We gave you a great review, we hope you'll do the same" is reciprocal pressure.

The fourth one is easy to miss. Don't tie any goodwill gesture to review timing. In OP.8, Maya gave a $100 credit when the internet went down. She sent it during the stay, with no mention of reviews. Keep it that way.

Your own review of the guest follows the same rules. Write it on the facts.

slides.title: Answer criticism for future guests: check the facts, fix what you can, then respond
items: Wait a day (house rule, not Airbnb's); don't reply while you're annoyed
Check the facts: turnover photos, the message thread, the friction log for that stay
Sort it: fair and fixable, fair but a known trade-off, or factually wrong
Fix what you can before you respond; never claim a fix that isn't done
Respond briefly: thank them, name the point, state the fix or fact; keep details private

box.label: Disputes are for policy violations
box.text: Hosts can dispute a review that breaks the policy; a dispute doesn't ensure removal. A retaliatory or extortion review may qualify. A fair three-star about a hot bunk room doesn't.

slides.notes:
A host's public response shows on the listing with the review. So you're writing for future guests, not arguing with the past one.

Wait a day. That's my house rule, not Airbnb's. Check the facts with the turnover photos, the message thread, and the friction log. Then sort the complaint.

Fair and fixable is the hot bunk room: respond with what you've fixed. Fair but a known trade-off: say a guest writes that the house is far from town. Thank them and point to where the listing already says so. Factually wrong: say a guest writes that an amenity wasn't listed when it was. State the fact calmly.

Fix what you can before you respond, and never claim a fix that isn't done. Then respond briefly.

Save disputes for policy violations. A review stays up unless its author asks for removal within 30 days, or it breaks the policy. A dispute doesn't guarantee removal. Disputing fair criticism wastes time, and it doesn't fix the house.

[Recording note: Preston can add a real example here if he has one.]

slides.title: Track seven metrics monthly, each with a definition, a target, and an owner
rows: Minutes from first message to a reply from a person or a reviewed template
Median under 15 min, 7 a.m. to 10 p.m.; every reply then under 60. After 10 p.m., auto-reply
Count by category: cleanliness, accuracy, check-in, amenities, noise, communication
Any category seen twice a quarter has a fix, owner, and date
Failed photo reviews plus guest reports
Zero; any miss gets a root-cause note
Record only; pushing it risks the no-pressure rule
Returning guests, "we'll be back," direct inquiries
Record and thank; never trade for reviews
slides.caption: Targets are Cedar Ridge house rules, not Airbnb thresholds. Sources: platform inbox or property management software (PMS), friction log, OP.8 records, reviews, Sam's OP.3 channel.
slides.notes:
Track the things you can act on, monthly. Each metric needs a definition, a target, and someone who owns it. These targets are Cedar Ridge house rules, not Airbnb thresholds. Set your own.

First response time runs to a reply from a person, or from a message template Maya has already reviewed. The aim is a median under 15 minutes from 7 a.m. to 10 p.m., and every reply in those hours under 60. After 10 p.m., an auto-reply gives the after-hours number.

Complaint reasons get counted by category. Any category seen twice in a quarter gets a fix, an owner, and a date.

Cleanliness misses and host cancellations both target zero.

Review rate has no target. Pushing it risks pressuring guests, so you just record it.

Rating distribution matters more than the average. Read every review below five stars. Any review below four stars also gets a check of the turnover photos and message thread within 48 hours.

Record repeat-stay signals and thank people. Never trade anything for a review.

slides.title: About 10 reviews in 90 days means each one is a tenth of what new guests read
slides.side:
61 stays is the base case. The 70% review rate is an assumption.

A full year: 61 × 70% = 42.7, about 43 reviews.

Actual launch months may be slower.
slides.notes:
Now the Cedar Ridge numbers. The base case expects 61 stays a year, about 5.1 a month.

In the first 90 days, that's 61 times 90 over 365. That's 15.04, so about 15 stays. Real launch months may be slower, so treat 15 as the base-case pace, not a promise.

If about 70% of guests leave a review, that's 15 times 0.7, which is 10.5. Call it 10 reviews in 90 days. The 70% is an assumption. Over a full year at the same rate, it's 61 times 0.7, about 43.

Why does this matter? Because ten reviews is a small sample. One three-star review is one in every ten reviews a new guest reads. That's why the tracker counts the distribution, not just the average. And it's why the complaint log matters so much early. With ten reviews, two people mentioning the same problem is a pattern.

The tracker on the next slides uses these numbers. All the tracker data are assumptions for teaching.

slides.title: A 4.6 average hides a three-star review that names a real problem
slides.text: Day-90 tracker: 10 reviews. Average (7 × 5 + 2 × 4 + 1 × 3) / 10 = 46 / 10 = 4.6. Complaint mentions come from reviews and messages: one bunk-room mention was in the three-star review, the other in a guest message.

items.label: Complaint mentions: bunk room too warm

slides.caption: Also at day 90: median first response 9 minutes, 14 of 15 under 60, one at 90 minutes after 10 p.m. Zero cleanliness misses, zero host cancellations, 2 "we'll be back" mentions, 1 inquiry about next summer.
slides.notes:
Here's the tracker at day 90. Remember, all these data are assumptions for teaching.

The top three bars are reviews. Seven are five-star, two are four-star, and one is three-star. The average is 46 divided by 10, which is 4.6. That looks fine.

The bottom three bars are complaint mentions, from reviews and messages together. Two guests mentioned a warm bunk room. One said it in the three-star review, and the other said it in a message. That's a repeat, so it goes on the fix list.

One guest found the check-in directions unclear. One hit the internet outage from OP.8.

The response times look good. The median is 9 minutes, and 14 of 15 threads got a reply within an hour. One took 90 minutes, and it came in after 10 p.m.

Cleanliness misses and host cancellations are zero. There are two "we'll be back" mentions and one inquiry about next summer.

So skip the debate about whether 4.6 is good. Ask what the three-star review and the complaints are telling you to fix.

slides.title: The day-90 tracker produces four fixes, and the repeat complaint comes first
rows: Bunk room too warm (2 mentions); no dedicated cooling
Quote a ceiling fan or portable unit; over the $200 limit, so owner decision list. Meanwhile: thermostat line in the manual, note in the listing
Check-in directions unclear; map app routes guests down a closed lake road
Photo of the correct turnoff in the 7-day message and the house manual
Keep safety messages on the after-hours phone; add an after-hours auto-reply with that number
Cellular backup router quote, already on the owner decision list (OP.8)
slides.notes:
This is how the Cedar Ridge team reads the day-90 tracker.

The bunk room comes first, because it's a repeat. The lower level has no dedicated cooling in the bunk room. Chris gets a quote for a ceiling fan or a portable cooling unit. Either costs more than $200, the most the team can spend on one item without the owners' OK. So it goes on the owner decision list. That's the purchases Maya and Chris decide at their month-end review. Until then, the house manual adds a line on thermostat settings, and the listing adds a note. Accuracy covers comfort too.

The unclear directions come from a mapping app that routes guests down a closed lake road. Maya adds a photo of the correct turnoff to the 7-day message and the house manual.

The 90-minute reply came in after 10 p.m., outside Maya's messaging hours, so it's outside the target. Safety messages still go to the after-hours phone. A new auto-reply gives that number.

The internet fix was already queued in OP.8. Two owner decisions are now pending: backup internet and bunk room cooling.

slides.title: Say a fix is done in public only once it's really done

left.head: The three-star review
items: "Great lake access and clean house, but the bunk room was really hot and the kids didn't sleep well."
Fair, specific, and useful
Don't dispute it

right.head: The response, once cooling is in
items: "Thanks for staying with us and for the specific feedback on the bunk room. You're right that the lower level ran warm. We've added cooling to the bunk room and updated the house manual with thermostat tips for the lower level. We're glad you enjoyed the lake."
Not approved yet? Wait, or say only what's done: the manual line and the listing note

slides.notes:
Suppose the three-star review reads: "Great lake access and clean house, but the bunk room was really hot and the kids didn't sleep well."

Run the process. Wait a day. Check the facts: the complaint log already shows the same issue in another guest's message. Sort it: fair and fixable. Fix what you can. Then respond.

The response thanks them and names the specific point. It agrees where they're right. It states the fix: cooling added, and thermostat tips in the manual. It ends on something true and positive about the stay.

That response is only accurate once the cooling is actually installed. If the owners haven't approved it yet, wait to post. Or post a version that says only what's done: the manual line and the listing note. A response that claims a fix that isn't there becomes its own accuracy problem.

Don't dispute this review. It's fair, specific, and useful.

What goes to Sam's OP.10: the 90-day tracker, the complaint log with fixes and dates, the response-time data, and the pending owner decisions.

slides.title: Map each search factor to one thing you'll check every month
slides.caption: Part A of the exercise. The same blank table is in the written lesson, section OP.9.9.
slides.notes:
The exercise has three parts. This is Part A, your factor map.

For each factor from Airbnb's search page, write what you control, one thing you'll check every month, and who checks it.

Quality gets three rows, because it covers the most ground: photos and listing accuracy, reviews, and communication. Then popularity, price, and availability.

Price is a shared row. You fill it in with what you bring back from Sam's OP.5, not with a guess. Availability ties back to your permit, so check your minimum stays against it.

Keep each monthly check small and concrete. "Compare listing photos to the house" works. "Improve quality" doesn't. If you can't say who does the check, it won't happen.

Part B, on the next slide, is your review request.

slides.title: Check your review request against five questions before it ever sends
rows: Doesn't link to any refund, deposit, discount, or future stay
Sent after checkout, not tied to a goodwill gesture
slides.caption: Part B of the exercise. Parts A (factor map) and C (monthly tracker) are blank tables in the written lesson, section OP.9.9.
slides.notes:
Part B is your review request. Write it first. Then run it through these five checks. Every answer should be yes. If any answer is no, rewrite it.

The first two are the core of the policy. Offer nothing of value, and don't name a rating.

The third check catches a lot of people. The request can't link to a refund, a deposit, a discount, or a future stay. Even a friendly "hope to see you next summer, here's a code" in the same message reads as a trade.

The fourth check makes sure you still hear about problems. The fifth keeps any goodwill gesture separate from the request.

Part C is the monthly tracker, and it's a blank table in the written lesson. One row per month covers stays, reviews, star counts, median first response, and complaints by reason. It also covers cleaning misses, host cancellations, repeat signals, and a fix list with an item, an owner, and a date. Start it on your first booking. Sam's OP.10 review uses it.

slides.title: Four rules turn the tracker into decisions instead of a monthly report

gates.q: Has every complaint reason seen twice this quarter got a fix, an owner, and a date?
gates.no: Put it on the fix list now

gates.q: Have you read the turnover photos and message thread for every review below four stars within 48 hours?
gates.no: Read them before doing anything else

gates.q: Are the facts checked, and is every fix you mention really done?
gates.sub: Only then post a response that says it's fixed.
gates.no: Wait, or say only what's already done

gates.q: Does the review break Airbnb's reviews policy?
gates.sub: Save the policy section you rely on.
gates.no: Don't dispute it; fix the house instead

slides.end: A tracker that doesn't change the fix list is just a record.
slides.notes:
These are the decision rules from the exercise, written as four questions. If the answer is no, do what the box on the right says.

First: has every complaint reason that showed up twice this quarter got a fix, an owner, and a date? If not, put it on the fix list now. At Cedar Ridge, that's the bunk room.

Second: have you read the turnover photos and message thread for every review below four stars, within 48 hours? The 48 hours is my house rule. Pick a window and keep to it. If not, read them before you do anything else.

Third: are the facts checked, and is every fix you mention really done? If not, wait, or say only what's already done.

Fourth: does the review break Airbnb's reviews policy? If not, don't dispute it. Fix the house instead. If you do dispute one, save the policy section you're relying on.

Every month, look at whether the fix list changed. If the tracker never moves the fix list, it isn't doing its job.

slides.title: Before you change your listing for search, check the current rules
rows: The search, ground rules, and reviews pages change; reread them before relying on any wording here
Any change to minimum stays or open dates must fit your permit's conditions

box.label: The standing rule
box.text: A ranking claim needs an Airbnb page behind it. If there isn't one, it doesn't go in the listing plan.

slides.notes:
Two checks before you change anything.

First, Airbnb's current pages. The search page, the ground rules, and the reviews policy all change. I checked them in September 2026. Before you rely on any wording here, open the current page and read it yourself.

Second, your local licensing office. Availability and stay flexibility help a listing show up. But if you shorten your minimum stay or open more dates to help search, that change has to stay within your permit's conditions. Ask before you change them.

And the rule I'd keep on the wall: a ranking claim needs an Airbnb page behind it. If there isn't one, it doesn't go in your plan.

[Production note: Sam confirms before recording that nothing here overlaps or conflicts with his OP.2 lesson on listing optimization and structured data.]

slides.title: This week, write your review request and start the monthly tracker
items: Read Airbnb's search page and fill in your factor map.
Write your review request and pass it through all five checks.
Start a friction log in a shared note or spreadsheet.
Set up the monthly tracker, including a fix list.
slides.next: Next: Sam's OP.10. Bring your tracker, complaint log, and pending owner decisions.
slides.notes:
Four short actions.

Read Airbnb's search page yourself. Then fill in the factor map for your listing.

Write your review request. Run it through the five checks. Put it in your scheduled messages for two or three days after checkout.

Start a friction log. A shared note or a spreadsheet is enough. If you already have guests, go back through last month's messages and mark every question.

Set up the monthly tracker. Keep it simple, and start it with your next booking.

Next in order is Sam's OP.10, The 30-Day and 90-Day Performance Review. Bring him your 90-day tracker, your complaint log, and your pending owner decisions. Watch for how he compares actual revenue, occupancy, and expenses with the PA.4 underwriting. That's the spreadsheet estimate of what the property would earn and cost, made before buying.

Then come back to OP.11, Scaling Your Portfolio. There I'll use that review to decide whether Cedar Ridge has earned a second property, or needs another season first.

box.label: Cedar Ridge figures
box.text: Cedar Ridge base case: 61 stays a year (the course's shared example numbers). The 90-day tracker values and the 70% review rate are teaching assumptions.

slides.notes:
Every rule in this lesson about search and reviews comes from Airbnb's own pages. I checked them on 2026-09-25 through search summaries, because direct fetches were blocked.

The search page, article 39, is the source for the factors: quality, popularity, price, location, variety, availability, and stay flexibility. The ground rules page covers accuracy, reservation commitment, communication, and cleanliness, and how Airbnb enforces them.

The reviews policy, article 2673, is where the limits on incentives, pressure, and trades come from. The reviews-for-homes page gives the 14-day window. The response page covers public responses. The dispute page covers the 30-day author removal and the fact that a dispute doesn't guarantee removal.

The resource center article supports the point that guests filter by amenities.

The only Cedar Ridge base-case number here is 61 stays a year, from the course's shared example numbers. Everything in the 90-day tracker, including the 70% review rate, is a teaching assumption. Your own tracker replaces it.
